title: Does a fixed d-to-1 Games conjecture imply Unique Games?
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Is the following implication true for the classical constraint games and deterministic polynomial reductions defined below?
\[\bigl(\exists\,d\in\mathbb N,\ d\ge2\text{ and }D_d\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{UGC}.\]
Here \(D_d\) is the perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one Games conjecture with \(d\) fixed independently of the soundness parameter; \(\mathrm{UGC}\) is the full near-perfect-completeness Unique Games conjecture. Equivalently, for every fixed \(d\ge2\), does \(D_d\) imply \(\mathrm{UGC}\)? The card retains the forward implication singled out in the saved source excerpt.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether the d-to-one conjecture implies the Unique Games conjecture, and separately whether the reverse implication holds.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the full paragraph on page 15:3; the card keeps the forward direction in its inherited excerpt

why: An implication would connect exact satisfiability in many-to-one constraint games with the near-satisfiable permutation games used to predict sharp approximation thresholds. The new perfect-completeness four-to-one claim makes this relationship especially consequential: accepting that theorem would make the requested implication as strong as full UGC.
status_note: Source-open as a full implication to UGC. progress.text: The source explicitly leaves both conjecture implications open and proves the forward implication only to its weaker one-sided Unique Games conjecture, with completeness 1/d.
The two-to-one proof sequence establishes an almost-perfect-completeness result; the 2025 journal account continues to distinguish full UGC and perfect-completeness d-to-one hardness.
A new preprint claims D₄ with exact perfect completeness. Its stated main theorem establishes the antecedent if correct, but does not establish the Unique Games conclusion.

sentences: The question asks whether perfect-completeness d-to-one hardness for any fixed d implies the full Unique Games conjecture.
Every game is an explicit finite classical constraint system, and hardness means deterministic polynomial reductions from Boolean satisfiability.
Known direct conversion gives a fixed positive Unique Games completeness rather than a value arbitrarily close to one.
A September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness four-to-one hardness, which would establish the antecedent if correct.
The implication remains a separate target and, conditional on that theorem, is equivalent to proving full UGC.

definitions:
A constraint game has two finite disjoint vertex sets \(U,V\) and a nonempty finite list of edges \(e=(u_e,v_e)\in U\times V\). Repeated edges, with their own constraints, are allowed and count separately. Every edge has equal weight in the list. No regularity or bounded-degree promise is imposed. All vertices, edges and constraint tables are explicitly encoded with binary integers; there is no succinct representation or compressed multiplicity.

For integers \(d\ge2\) and \(r\ge1\), a \(d\)-to-one game gives left vertices labels in \([dr]\), right vertices labels in \([r]\), and every edge a surjective map \(\pi_e:[dr]\to[r]\) with exactly \(d\) preimages of every right label. Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). An assignment is a pair of maps \(\alpha:U\to[dr]\) and \(\beta:V\to[r]\); it satisfies edge \(e\) when \(\pi_e(\alpha(u_e))=\beta(v_e)\). Its value is the fraction of list entries it satisfies. The optimum \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the maximum of this fraction over all assignments. It lies in \([0,1]\) and is a finite rational maximum. Perfect completeness means the YES instance has optimum exactly one.

A Unique Game has the same bipartite constraint format, a common alphabet \([k]\) on both sides, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[k]\to[k]\) on each edge. Assignment, satisfaction and optimum are defined by the same equality. This is a classical combinatorial optimum; no entangled, interactive, nonsignalling or quantum strategy is used.

For a promised pair of disjoint YES and NO sets of such instances, NP-hard means that Boolean 3-SAT has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to that pair. Specifically, a single finite Turing program maps every explicitly encoded Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause to a valid game. It maps satisfiable formulas into YES and unsatisfiable formulas into NO and uses at most \(K(L+1)^c\) bit steps on every length-\(L\) input, for fixed constants \(K,c\). Literal indices, signs, clauses, vertex names and table entries use ordinary explicit binary encodings. An algorithm for the promised game need have no specified behaviour outside YES and NO. NP-hardness here asserts the existence of a reduction; it does not assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

For a fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \(D_d\) to mean:
\[\forall\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1),\ \exists r\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapD}_{d,r}(1,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard},\]
where the YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\) and the NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The integer \(d\) is outside the quantifier over \(\gamma\). The alphabet size \(r\), reduction program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(d,\gamma\), but not on the formula length. Allowing \(d\) to increase as \(\gamma\) decreases would be a different antecedent.

Define full \(\mathrm{UGC}\) by
\[\forall\eta,\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/4),\ \exists k\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapUG}_{k}(1-\eta,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard}.\]
Its YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\eta\) and its NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The constants \(k\) and the polynomial reduction may depend on both gap parameters. The rational, small-gap convention gives disjoint promises and is equivalent to requesting all arbitrarily small positive gaps: smaller rational gaps imply the less stringent real gaps. There is no demand for one alphabet or one polynomial degree working for all gap choices, or for a uniform algorithm generating all the reductions from their parameters.

The target is the implication between these mathematical hardness propositions. It is not a question about formal unprovability in a separately chosen axiom system, nor is it limited to one specified family of gadget or oracle reductions. The reverse implication from UGC to perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one hardness is a separate question mentioned in the source, not an additional requirement on this card.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative answer must establish full UGC from the assumption that \(D_d\) holds for some fixed \(d\ge2\), respecting the gap quantifiers and the deterministic polynomial reductions. An unconditional proof of UGC would also establish the implication. A negative answer must prove the conjunction \((\exists d\ge2\ D_d)\land\neg\mathrm{UGC}\); showing only that a particular reduction loses completeness, or that some restricted reduction class cannot work, does not refute the implication. Hardness of Unique Games with a fixed YES value such as \(1/d\) or \(1/2\) is not the required near-one YES value for every \(\eta>0\). Exact asymptotic proof is required; the numerical approximation tolerance does not alter these logical statements.

context_blocks.text: Both games ask for globally consistent labels subject to local compatibility rules. Unique Games has one allowed right label for each left label and also one allowed left label for each right label. A d-to-one constraint keeps the first property but permits d compatible left labels for a given right label. This additional freedom changes which perfect-completeness gaps are possible.

The source already proves a weaker implication: its Appendix B gives one-sided Unique Games hardness with completeness 1/d. This is one fixed positive completeness constant. Full UGC instead requires a YES value arbitrarily close to one while keeping soundness arbitrarily close to zero. The weaker implication therefore does not answer the source question.

Perfectly satisfiable Unique Games can be checked efficiently by trying a starting label in each connected component and propagating the forced labels. The conjecture deliberately permits a small positive fraction of unsatisfied constraints in the YES case. Substituting exact satisfiability for near-satisfiability would change the problem.

The 2025 journal account explains the sequence that proved almost-perfect-completeness two-to-one hardness. It retains exact perfect completeness as a separate conjecture and states full UGC separately. These distinctions matter even though all the parameters may be described informally as almost satisfiable games.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness four-to-one hardness for every positive soundness constant. If correct, its Theorem 1.6 establishes D₄ and hence the antecedent of this card. Under that theorem, the forward implication is equivalent to UGC itself: an implication proof would give UGC, while UGC immediately implies the implication. This is a logical consequence of the claimed theorem, not a claim that UGC has been proved. The new full proof has not been independently audited here.

This connection would turn a hardness theorem with several compatible labels into the general Unique Games hypothesis underlying many sharp approximation thresholds. Keeping alphabet size, constraint multiplicity, completeness and soundness explicit prevents a useful weaker hardness theorem from being mistaken for that conclusion.
